title: Pressure on top of my head: daily headache with neck stiffness in a 26-year-old PhD student in general practice
desc: This station involves a focused headache history and a focused neurological, head and neck examination of James, a 26-year-old PhD student seen in general practice. For the past 6 weeks he has had a daily pressing headache that builds through the day, with neck and shoulder stiffness, while he writes his thesis. The candidate screens for red flags and features of other headache types, and finds that he takes analgesics most days. They then interpret his observations and a K10 questionnaire, diagnose tension-type headache, explain why no investigations are needed, and plan simple analgesia with limits to prevent medication-overuse headache, posture and lifestyle measures, stress support, smoking cessation, follow-up and safety netting.
focus: Taking a structured headache history that screens for red flags, diagnosing tension-type headache and managing it without overusing analgesics
diagnosis: Tension-type headache, currently daily for 6 weeks (on a background of occasional episodic TTH; at risk of chronic TTH, which needs ≥15 days/month for >3 months)
Psychological distress from thesis stress; smoking
stem: You are a medical student on your general practice rotation. James, a 26-year-old PhD student, has come in today because of headaches. Your GP supervisor will see him after you.
tasks: Take a focused history from James and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you James's observations and the K10 questionnaire he completed in the waiting room. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are James, a 26-year-old PhD student. It is a late-afternoon appointment and you have a headache right now, as you do every afternoon. You are tired, a bit tense and keen to get back to your thesis. You rub the back of your neck from time to time. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: “I’ve been getting these headaches every day lately and they’re really getting in the way of my work.”

The headache (give only when asked):

  • Site: all over your head, but mostly on top. Both sides, never just one.
  • Radiation: it spreads down into the back of your neck.
  • Onset and timing: it is never there when you wake up. It comes on slowly later in the day, usually from about early afternoon, gets worse as the day goes on, and lasts until you go to bed. You are fine again the next morning. It has never come on suddenly. Progression (give if asked whether it is getting worse): it has stayed about the same, 5 to 6 out of 10, every day for the 6 weeks. It is not getting more severe, lasting longer or starting earlier in the day.
  • How long this has been going on: every day for about the last 6 weeks, since you started writing up your thesis full-time. Before that you had the odd mild headache at busy times, a couple a month, but nothing like this.
  • Character: a pressure-like ache, “like something pressing on my head”. Not throbbing or pounding.
  • Severity: 5 to 6 out of 10. It is about a 5 now.
  • What helps: resting, lying down and Panadol.
  • What makes it worse: stress, and long hours sitting at your desk. Cycling home does not make it worse. It is not worse with coughing, sneezing, straining, bending over or lying down.
  • Neck and shoulders: your neck and shoulders are sore and stiff, worse as the day goes on.
  • Impact: when the pain and stiffness build up you cannot concentrate or sit at your desk any longer.

Say no if asked about:

  • a sudden severe headache that hit like a thunderclap, the worst headache of your life, collapse or fainting;
  • fever, feeling unwell, a rash, or pain or stiffness when bending your head forward (your neck is sore and tight, but you can put your chin on your chest);
  • headaches that wake you or are worst first thing in the morning, vomiting, weight loss, night sweats;
  • weakness, numbness or tingling, trouble speaking, blurred, double or lost vision, confusion or seizures;
  • throbbing pain, pain on one side, nausea, sensitivity to light or noise, flashing or zigzag lights before the headache;
  • pain around one eye, a red or watering eye, a runny or blocked nose, a droopy eyelid, or pacing about during the pain;
  • a head injury or a fall from your bike (you always wear a helmet);
  • jaw pain when chewing or a tender scalp;
  • recent travel or recent illness.

Past medical history: appendix out at 19. Asthma since childhood, mild: you use your puffer a few times a year, mostly in hay fever season, though you have been a bit more chesty lately when you have been smoking more. Hay fever.

Medicines:

  • Salbutamol (Ventolin) puffer when needed.
  • Panadol and Nurofen for the headaches. Only if asked how often: Panadol, 2 tablets, on most days, about 5 days a week for the last 6 weeks, and you add Nurofen, 2 tablets, once or twice a week when Panadol is not enough. Nurofen has never made your breathing worse (say so if asked). No other painkillers, and nothing with codeine.
  • No other medicines or supplements. No recreational drugs.

Allergies: dust mites, cats and pollen (they set off your hay fever and sometimes your asthma). No medicine allergies.

Family history: your mother has eczema and asthma. Your father has high blood pressure. Your sister has asthma. Nobody in the family gets bad headaches.

Social history:

  • Smoking: a social smoker, a few cigarettes on a night out, but lately 3 or 4 a day because of the stress.
  • Alcohol: a glass of red wine most weeknights, two or more when you are stressed.
  • Coffee (only if asked): one coffee in the morning.
  • Study: PhD student. Your thesis is due in 3 months. You sit at your laptop most of the day and into the evening, often without breaks.
  • Sleep (only if asked): late nights writing, about 6 hours a night.
  • Activity and diet: you cycle to university. You meal prep your dinners but usually eat out at lunch.
  • Travel: none.
  • Home and supports: you live alone in a studio near the university. Your family is interstate. Your girlfriend is also a student, and you have close friends. “I’m pretty stressed at the moment.”
  • Mood (only if asked): stressed and a bit flat with the workload, but you do not feel depressed and you still enjoy time with your girlfriend and friends. No thoughts of harming yourself.

Ideas, concerns and expectations:

  • Idea: “I wonder if it’s the workload and stress from writing my thesis.”
  • Concern (say this when asked what worries you): “I’m worried I won’t finish my thesis on time. And the stress makes the headaches worse.”
  • Expectation: something to get rid of the headaches so you can keep working, ideally “something stronger than Panadol”.

Question to raise near the end of Part 1: “It’s nothing serious, is it?” Accept a brief answer, or a promise to come back to it once the results are back.

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they are examining):

  • General inspection: alert, well, a little tired. Sits with his head forward and shoulders rounded. Not pale or flushed. No rash.
  • Observations: the practice nurse has done them: temperature 36.6 °C, BP 126/78 mmHg, HR 72/min regular, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air. (The full set is handed over in Part 2.)
  • Meningism: passive neck flexion full, chin to chest, with no resistance or pain. Kernig’s sign negative. Brudzinski negative (if tested).
  • Fundoscopy: optic discs pink with sharp margins, no swelling. Spontaneous venous pulsations present. No haemorrhages.
  • Eyes and cranial nerves: visual acuity 6/6 in each eye. Visual fields full to confrontation. Pupils equal and reactive, no ptosis or miosis, no red or watering eye. Eye movements full, no nystagmus or double vision. Facial sensation and movement normal. Palate, tongue and shoulder shrug normal.
  • Limbs: no pronator drift. Tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical. Plantars flexor.
  • Coordination and gait: finger-nose and heel-shin normal. Gait normal, including heel-to-toe walking. Romberg negative.
  • Head and neck muscles: tender and tight on palpation of the upper trapezius, the muscles at the base of the skull and the temporalis on both sides. Pressing there reproduces his familiar ache.
  • Neck movements: full range in all directions, with discomfort at the end of rotation to both sides. No midline spinal tenderness.
  • Other: temporal arteries pulsatile and non-tender. No scalp tenderness. Sinuses non-tender. Jaw joints move normally and are not tender.
  • Chest (if examined): clear, no wheeze.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms James's identity, explains the examination and gains consent.
Empathic and non-judgemental: acknowledges the stress of his thesis deadline, asks about smoking and alcohol without judgement, and uses plain language.
History
Characterises the headache:

kids.x: Site and radiation: all over the head, mostly on top, on both sides, spreading into the neck.
Onset and timing: comes on slowly later in the day and builds until bedtime, never present on waking, never sudden; every day for about 6 weeks, with occasional mild headaches before that.
kids.d: Award only if the speed of onset and the duration of the daily pattern are both established.

kids.x: Character and severity: a pressure-like, non-throbbing ache, 5 to 6/10.
Relieving and aggravating factors: rest, lying down and Panadol help; worse with stress and long desk hours; not worse with cycling.

check.x: Asks about associated symptoms and finds neck and shoulder pain and stiffness that build through the day.
Asks about the impact: cannot concentrate or sit at his desk once the pain and stiffness build.
Screens for red flags of a secondary headache:

kids.x: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: sudden thunderclap onset, worst headache ever, collapse [no].
Meningitis: fever, rash, photophobia, pain on bending the head forward [no].
Raised intracranial pressure or tumour: progressively worsening over the weeks, wakes him or worst on waking, worse with coughing, straining or lying down, vomiting, weight loss or night sweats [no].
Stroke or TIA: weakness, numbness, speech or vision disturbance, confusion or seizures [no].
Head injury, including falls from his bike [no].

check.x: Asks about features of other primary headaches: migraine (throbbing, one-sided, nausea, light or noise sensitivity, aura) and cluster headache (one-sided pain around the eye, red watering eye, runny nose, droopy eyelid, restlessness) [all absent].
check.d: Award only if features of both migraine and cluster headache are asked about.

check.x: Takes the past medical history and allergies: appendicectomy at 19, mild asthma, hay fever; allergic to dust mites, cats and pollen; no medicine allergies.
Takes a medication history:

kids.x: Salbutamol puffer when needed, used a few times a year.
Quantifies analgesic use: Panadol on about 5 days a week and Nurofen once or twice a week for 6 weeks; no codeine.
kids.d: Award only if the number of days a week (or a month) is established, not just the drug names.

kids.x: Asks whether Nurofen worsens his asthma [no].

check.x: Takes a family history: mother eczema and asthma, father hypertension, sister asthma; no family history of severe headaches.
check.d: Award for asking about family history including headaches.

check.x: Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking and alcohol, quantified: social smoker, now 3 or 4 a day when stressed; a glass of red wine most weeknights, more when stressed.
Study and work habits: PhD thesis due in 3 months, long hours at a laptop without breaks, late nights with about 6 hours' sleep.
Home, activity and supports: lives alone, cycles to university, girlfriend and close friends, family interstate.
kids.d: Award for living situation, supports and activity; diet and travel not required.

check.x: Screens mood and safety: stressed and a bit flat, not depressed, still enjoys time with others, no thoughts of self-harm.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is thesis stress, worried he will not finish on time, wants something stronger than Panadol so he can keep working.
Examination
Asks for the observations, including blood pressure and temperature [BP 126/78, temperature 36.6 °C, all normal].
General inspection, including posture [well; forward head and rounded shoulders; no rash].
Examines for meningism: passive neck flexion and Kernig's sign [negative], distinguishing it from muscular neck stiffness.
Performs fundoscopy to look for papilloedema [sharp discs, spontaneous venous pulsations present].
Examines the cranial nerves: acuity, visual fields, pupils (including ptosis and miosis), eye movements, facial sensation and movement [all normal].
Examines the limbs for a focal deficit: pronator drift, tone, power, reflexes, sensation and plantars; gait and coordination [normal].
check.d: Award for a screening limb neurological examination including power, reflexes and either plantars or pronator drift.

check.x: Palpates the pericranial, neck and shoulder muscles and assesses neck range of movement [tender, tight trapezius, suboccipital and temporalis muscles reproducing his ache; full range with end-range discomfort].
Checks the temporal arteries, scalp, sinuses and jaw joints [all normal].
check.d: Award if at least two are checked.

check.x: Interpretation
Interprets the observations as normal: afebrile and normotensive on repeat, so no sign of infection or a hypertensive cause; no escalation needed.

Adds up the K10 to a total of 20 and interprets it as moderate psychological distress, in keeping with his thesis stress, and links it to offering psychological support; notes that the K10 is a screen, not a diagnosis.
check.d: Award for a correct total of 20 with the moderate band and linking it to psychological support; mentioning it is a screening tool is desirable, not required.

check.x: Gives tension-type headache as the most likely diagnosis, justified by a bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate headache not worsened by physical activity, without nausea, photophobia or phonophobia, with pericranial muscle tenderness, clear stress and posture triggers and a normal neurological examination.
check.d: Award for tension-type headache plus at least three supporting features (e.g. bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate, not worse with activity, no migraine features, pericranial tenderness, normal examination).

check.x: Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: migraine, cluster headache, medication-overuse headache, meningitis, raised intracranial pressure or a space-occupying lesion.
check.d: Award for at least three, including one dangerous cause, each justified.

check.x: States that no blood tests or brain imaging are needed: although the pattern has changed (new daily headache for 6 weeks), it has typical TTH features, a clear trigger, is not progressing in severity, there are no other red flags, and the examination including fundoscopy is normal; would investigate if it progresses or new features appear.
check.d: Award if the candidate states no blood tests or imaging are needed and justifies it with typical features or no red flags plus a normal examination including the fundi, with a plan to investigate if it changes. Do not award if CT or MRI is requested.

check.x: Management
Explains tension-type headache in plain language (a common headache linked to stress, posture and muscle tension) and reassures him honestly that it is not a sign of serious disease.
check.d: Award from the diagnosis answer, the reply to his scan question or the management answer.

check.x: Plans analgesia safely:

kids.x: Simple analgesia taken early in a headache: paracetamol 1 g or ibuprofen 400 mg (he tolerates NSAIDs despite his asthma); declines codeine or other opioids.
kids.d: Accept the drugs without exact doses; do not award if an opioid is offered.

kids.x: Explains medication-overuse headache: he already takes analgesics on most days, so he should limit them (simple analgesics on 15 or more days a month for over 3 months cause it).
kids.d: Accept fewer than 10 days a month or no more than 2 to 3 days a week; the candidate must link frequent use to medication-overuse headache.

check.x: Advises on posture and lifestyle, including physiotherapy for neck and shoulder tension, desk set-up and ergonomics, regular breaks from the screen, regular sleep, hydration and meals, and continuing exercise.

Addresses stress: offers psychological support: university counselling (free), or a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan with a psychologist if assessment shows a mental disorder (e.g. an adjustment disorder with anxiety); suggests talking to his supervisor about the thesis timeline.
check.d: Award for offering psychological support by either option (university counselling, or a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan if assessment shows a mental disorder); talking to his thesis supervisor is optional.

check.x: Gives brief smoking cessation advice and offers Quitline (13 7848); alcohol advice optional.
Safety netting

Names red flags in plain words with 000 or ED: a sudden severe headache that peaks within a minute, fever with a stiff neck or rash, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or vision loss, confusion or a seizure.
check.d: Award for a sudden severe headache plus at least two other red flags, with 000 or ED.

check.x: Advises seeing the GP sooner if the headaches change in pattern, start waking him or are worst on waking, come with vomiting, or keep needing painkillers on most days despite these measures.
Arranges follow-up: a headache and medicine diary and GP review in about 4 weeks.

part2.lead: Here are James's observations from the practice nurse and the K10 questionnaire he filled in in the waiting room.
part2.patient:
• When the candidate explains the diagnosis, ask: “So it’s nothing serious? I don’t need a scan?” Settle if the candidate explains clearly why not.
  • When painkillers come up: “Can’t you just give me something stronger? I really need to keep working.” Accept the advice if the candidate explains medication-overuse headache kindly.
  • If smoking is raised: “It’s the only thing that helps me relax at the moment.” Agree to think about Quitline if it is offered without judgement.

handover.label: Observations (practice nurse, today)
handover.result: Taken seated in the treatment room this afternoon, with a repeat BP after 10 minutes' rest. James has his usual headache at the time (it started at about 2 pm).
handover.model:
• Read: RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, HR 72 then 70 and regular, BP 126/78 then 124/76 mmHg, temperature 36.6 °C, alert, pain 5/10. Every value is within normal adult ranges (it would sit in the white zone of an adult observation chart if plotted), so no escalation is needed.
  • For James: afebrile, so no sign of meningitis or another infection. Normotensive on repeat (relevant with his father's hypertension), so not a hypertensive headache. Stable and well despite the headache.
  • What it changes: he can be managed in general practice. The normal observations support the absence of other red flags; with the typical features and a clear trigger for his change in pattern, no investigations are needed.

rows.note: Seated; headache present since about 2 pm

handover.label: K10 questionnaire (completed in the waiting room today)
handover.result:
Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10), self-completed by James in the waiting room. Each question asks about the last 4 weeks and is scored 1 (none of the time), 2 (a little of the time), 3 (some of the time), 4 (most of the time) or 5 (all of the time).

In the last 4 weeks, how often did you feel...Score
1. Tired out for no good reason3
2. Nervous3
3. So nervous that nothing could calm you down1
4. Hopeless1
5. Restless or fidgety3
6. So restless you could not sit still2
7. Depressed2
8. That everything was an effort3
9. So sad that nothing could cheer you up1
10. Worthless1

Score bands: 10 to 15 low, 16 to 21 moderate, 22 to 29 high, 30 to 50 very high psychological distress.
handover.model:
• Read: adds the ten items to a total of 20 out of 50, in the moderate distress band. The high-scoring items are tiredness, nervousness, restlessness and everything being an effort. Hopelessness, sadness and worthlessness score 1.
  • For James: this fits significant stress from his thesis deadline rather than a depressive picture, matching his history (stressed, not depressed, no thoughts of self-harm). Stress is a key trigger of his tension-type headache. The K10 is a screening tool, not a diagnosis.
  • What it changes: it supports offering psychological support (university counselling, or a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan with a psychologist if assessment shows a mental disorder) as part of headache management, and it gives a baseline to repeat at review.

ask: You are now handing over to your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of James, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of James now, here in general practice.
Before James goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: medical student; James, 26, PhD student.
  • Situation: 6 weeks of daily bilateral pressing headache, mostly on top, 5 to 6/10, building through the afternoon until bedtime, with neck and shoulder stiffness; affecting his thesis work.
  • Background: mild asthma, hay fever; Panadol about 5 days a week and Nurofen once or twice a week; smokes 3 or 4 a day when stressed, a glass of red wine most weeknights, more when stressed; thesis due in 3 months.
  • Assessment: pattern change explained by a clear trigger, no other red flags; no meningism, normal fundi and neurological examination; tender pericranial and neck muscles. Observations normal. K10 20, moderate distress. Tension-type headache, daily for 6 weeks (too recent for chronic TTH); at risk of medication-overuse headache.
  • Recommendation: no investigations; limit analgesics; posture, lifestyle, physiotherapy and psychology; smoking support; review in 4 weeks with a diary.

Most likely: tension-type headache, daily for 6 weeks on a background of episodic TTH, not yet meeting chronic TTH criteria (>3 months). For: bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate, not worse with cycling; no nausea, photophobia or phonophobia; tender pericranial muscles; stress and posture triggers; normal examination.

  • Migraine: against: not throbbing or one-sided, no nausea, light sensitivity or aura.
  • Cluster headache: against: not one-sided around the eye, lasts hours, no tearing, runny nose or restlessness.
  • Medication-overuse headache: for: analgesics on about 5 days a week (about 20 days a month), above the ≥15 days a month threshold for simple analgesics. Against: only 6 weeks of overuse (needs >3 months); at risk.
  • Meningitis: against: 6 weeks, afebrile, no meningism or rash.
  • Raised intracranial pressure / space-occupying lesion: for: new daily headache over 6 weeks. Against: never on waking, not worse with coughing, straining or lying down, no vomiting, sharp discs with venous pulsations, normal neurological examination.

1. Explain and reassure: tension-type headache; no scan or blood tests needed.
  2. Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g or ibuprofen 400 mg early in a headache; no codeine or opioids; limit to fewer than 10 days a month (about 2 days a week) to avoid medication-overuse headache.
  3. Posture, breaks, sleep, physio: desk ergonomics, regular screen breaks, regular sleep, meals and fluids, keep cycling; physiotherapy for neck and shoulder tension.
  4. Stress support: psychological support: university counselling (free), or a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan with a psychologist if assessment shows a mental disorder (e.g. an adjustment disorder with anxiety); talk to his supervisor about the timeline.
  5. Smoking: brief cessation advice and Quitline 13 7848.

• Call 000 or go to ED: a sudden severe headache that peaks within a minute; fever with a stiff neck or rash; weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or loss of vision; confusion or a seizure.
  • See the GP sooner: the headaches change, wake him or are worst on waking, come with vomiting, or still need painkillers on most days.
  • Medicines: painkillers on fewer than 10 days a month (about 2 days a week); no codeine.
  • Follow-up: headache and medicine diary; GP review in about 4 weeks (repeat the K10, consider prevention if headaches stay frequent).

ddx.for: A daily bilateral pressing headache of 5 to 6/10 that builds through the day, not worse with cycling, with neck and shoulder stiffness, tender pericranial muscles, thesis stress and long desk hours, and a normal examination.
Recurrent headaches triggered by stress and poor sleep in a young adult.
ddx.against: The pain is bilateral, pressing and moderate, not throbbing, with no nausea, light or noise sensitivity or aura, and it is not worsened by activity.

ddx.for: Daily headaches in a man who smokes and drinks alcohol.
ddx.against: The pain is bilateral and on top of the head rather than around one eye, lasts all afternoon and evening, and has no tearing, red eye, runny nose or restlessness.

ddx.for: He takes Panadol on about 5 days a week and Nurofen once or twice a week.
ddx.against: The overuse has lasted only 6 weeks (ICHD-3 needs regular overuse for more than 3 months). He is already above the frequency threshold, so it will develop if overuse continues.

ddx.for: Headache with neck pain and stiffness.
ddx.against: Six weeks of daily headache in someone who is well, afebrile, with no rash, photophobia or meningism and full passive neck flexion.

ddx.for: A new daily headache over 6 weeks.
ddx.against: Never on waking, not worse with coughing, straining or lying down, no vomiting, sharp discs with venous pulsations and a normal neurological examination.

guide:
In Part 1 give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. James reveals how often he takes analgesics only when asked how often, and his sleep and mood only when asked. The history should take about 6 minutes, leaving time for meningism, fundoscopy, a screening neurological examination and palpation of the neck and pericranial muscles. Accept a stated, briefly described examination. For item 19, the candidate should tell meningism (pain or resistance on passive neck flexion) apart from his muscular neck stiffness. The observations are given as values in Part 1, and the full set is handed over in Part 2.

In Part 2 hand over both results together and ask the four questions in order. The K10 total is not printed: the candidate should add up the items (20) for item 27. James asks about a scan, stronger painkillers and smoking while the candidate explains. Score item 30 (no investigations) from the diagnosis or management answer, or from the reply to his scan question. Score item 32 (explanation and reassurance) from the diagnosis answer, the reply to his scan question or the management answer. Score items 33 to 36 from the management answer. Item 33.2 and items 34 to 36 may also be earned in the fourth answer. Score the safety-netting items from the fourth question. If analgesic frequency was not established in Part 1, item 11.2 cannot be awarded, but item 33.2 can still be earned.

A high-performing candidate characterises the headache systematically, groups the red flag questions by diagnosis (SAH, meningitis, raised pressure, stroke, head injury) and asks about migraine and cluster features. They count how often he takes analgesics, and they find the stress, smoking and poor sleep. They examine for meningism, papilloedema and focal signs and find the tender pericranial muscles. In Part 2 they diagnose tension-type headache, recognise the change in pattern and explain why, with a clear trigger, typical features and a normal examination, no investigations are needed. They decline codeine, explain the risk of medication-overuse headache, give practical posture, stress and smoking advice and clear red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic pain history and never asks how often he takes painkillers. They skip fundoscopy or meningism, order a CT “to be sure”, prescribe codeine or daily analgesia without a limit, or give vague safety netting (“come back if it gets worse”).
explain:
Approach to headache

First separate a primary headache (tension-type, migraine, cluster) from a secondary headache caused by another disease. Use the cardinal features of the pain (site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms, timing, exacerbating and relieving factors, severity), the impact on daily life, and questions grouped by diagnosis:

  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: a thunderclap headache that peaks within a minute, often with collapse or vomiting.
  • Meningitis: fever, neck stiffness, rash, photophobia, drowsiness.
  • Raised intracranial pressure or tumour: headache that wakes the patient or is worst on waking, worse with coughing, straining or lying down, vomiting, new neurological signs, weight loss, night sweats or a cancer history.
  • Stroke or TIA: sudden weakness, numbness, speech or visual loss.
  • Temporal arteritis: new headache over 50, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness.
  • Others: head injury, a new or changed pattern, immunosuppression, pregnancy.

Then ask about the features of the other primary headaches (migraine and cluster) and stratify the risk. James's pattern has changed (a couple of mild headaches a month before, now a daily headache for 6 weeks), which is a red flag that calls for a careful history and examination. In his case it has a clear trigger (full-time thesis writing), typical tension-type features, no progression in severity and no other red flags, and his examination including fundoscopy is normal. So no blood tests or imaging are needed, but he should be investigated if the headache progresses or new features appear.

Why James has tension-type headache

ICHD-3 defines tension-type headache as lasting 30 minutes to 7 days, with at least two of: bilateral location, a pressing or tightening (non-pulsating) quality, mild or moderate intensity, and no worsening with routine physical activity. There is no nausea or vomiting, and no more than one of photophobia or phonophobia. James has all four features, none of the associated symptoms, and tender pericranial muscles on palpation. Episodes are classed as infrequent (less than 1 day a month), frequent (1 to 14 days a month) or chronic (15 or more days a month for more than 3 months). His previous headaches (a couple a month) fit episodic TTH; the current daily pattern is too recent to meet chronic TTH criteria, so he is at risk of it. His triggers are typical: stress, long hours at a laptop with poor posture, few breaks, late nights, and more smoking and alcohol when stressed.

Differentials

  • Migraine: unilateral, pulsating, moderate to severe, worse with activity, with nausea or photophobia and phonophobia, sometimes with aura. James has none of these.
  • Cluster headache: strictly one-sided orbital pain for 15 to 180 minutes, with tearing, a red eye, rhinorrhoea, ptosis and restlessness. It is more common in men who smoke, but his headache does not fit.
  • Medication-overuse headache: headache on 15 or more days a month in someone with a pre-existing headache disorder, from regular overuse for more than 3 months of simple analgesics on 15 or more days a month, or triptans, opioids, combination analgesics or several drug classes combined on 10 or more days a month. James is already over the frequency threshold but has overused for only 6 weeks, so he does not yet meet the criteria; this is why limiting analgesics now matters.
  • Meningitis, SAH, raised ICP and stroke: excluded clinically by the gradual daily pattern, the absence of fever, meningism, morning or Valsalva features and focal symptoms, and a normal examination, including the fundi.

The results

His observations are normal: he is afebrile and normotensive on repeat, so there is no infective or hypertensive cause. His K10 items add up to 20, moderate psychological distress, matching his thesis stress without features of depression. It supports offering psychological support as part of the headache plan and is a baseline to repeat.

Management (eTG Neurology)

  • Explanation and reassurance: explaining the diagnosis and why no tests are needed is itself part of treatment.
  • Acute treatment: paracetamol 1 g or an NSAID such as ibuprofen 400 mg, taken early in a headache. NSAIDs and aspirin can worsen asthma in a minority of people, so check his tolerance (he takes Nurofen without problems). Avoid codeine and other opioids, which work poorly and promote medication-overuse headache. Keep acute treatment to fewer than 10 days a month (about 2 days a week).
  • Non-drug measures: posture and desk ergonomics, regular screen breaks, regular sleep, meals and fluids, regular exercise, and relaxation. Physiotherapy can help neck and shoulder tension. Psychological therapies such as CBT and stress management help frequent tension-type headache: offer university counselling (free), or a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan with a psychologist if assessment shows a mental disorder (e.g. an adjustment disorder with anxiety). Stress alone does not make him eligible for a Mental Health Treatment Plan.
  • Prevention: if headaches stay frequent or become chronic despite these measures, low-dose amitriptyline at night can be considered at review.
  • Smoking and alcohol: brief advice (Ask, Advise, Help), noting that smoking also worsens his asthma, with Quitline (13 7848) and pharmacotherapy. Keep alcohol within the NHMRC guideline of no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day.
  • Diary: a headache and medicine diary shows triggers and analgesic days, and measures the response.

Safety netting

James should call 000 or go to ED for a sudden severe headache that peaks within a minute, fever with a stiff neck or rash, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or loss of vision, confusion or a seizure. He should see the GP sooner if the pattern changes, the headaches wake him or are worst on waking, he starts vomiting, or he still needs painkillers on most days. Review in about 4 weeks with the diary.
points: Separate primary from secondary headache by grouping your red flag questions by diagnosis: SAH (thunderclap onset), meningitis (fever, rash, neck stiffness), raised pressure or tumour (progressive, worst on waking, worse with coughing or straining, vomiting), stroke or TIA, and head injury.

Tension-type headache is bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate and not worsened by activity, with no nausea and no more than one of photophobia or phonophobia. Pericranial muscle tenderness and stress and posture triggers support it.
Tell muscular neck stiffness apart from meningism: full, painless passive neck flexion and a negative Kernig's sign argue against meningeal irritation.

Always count analgesic days. Simple analgesics on 15 or more days a month (or opioids, triptans or combination analgesics on 10 or more) for over 3 months cause medication-overuse headache, so keep acute treatment to fewer than 10 days a month and avoid codeine.

A new or changed headache pattern is a red flag that needs a careful history and examination. When it has a clear trigger, typical primary headache features, no progression, no other red flags and a normal examination including fundoscopy, no imaging or blood tests are needed; investigate if it progresses or new features appear.
Treat tension-type headache mainly without drugs: posture and ergonomics, breaks, sleep, exercise, physiotherapy and stress management, with smoking cessation and a headache diary.
